mainEntity.name: Is it normal to feel a slight edge around my veneer?

acceptedAnswer.text: Immediately after veneer placement, a very slight margin may occasionally be perceptible as the surrounding tissues settle. However, if you notice a new or worsening edge, gap, or rough sensation around a veneer that was previously smooth, this is worth discussing with your dentist. Small changes at veneer margins can allow bacteria to accumulate, and early assessment helps ensure any issues are addressed before they become more complex. A clinician can examine the margin and determine whether any action is needed.

mainEntity.name: Can a gap around a veneer cause tooth decay?

acceptedAnswer.text: A gap or rough margin around a veneer can potentially allow plaque and bacteria to accumulate in an area that is difficult to clean effectively. Over time, if bacteria are not removed through regular brushing and flossing, there is an increased risk of decay developing at the tooth-veneer junction or beneath the veneer. This is one of the key reasons why professional monitoring of veneer margins during routine dental check-ups is recommended. Early detection of marginal changes allows treatment before decay has an opportunity to progress.

mainEntity.name: Will my veneer fall off if there is a gap around it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. A gap at the edge of a veneer does not automatically mean the veneer is about to detach. Many veneers remain well bonded to the majority of the tooth surface even when a marginal gap has developed. However, if the bond is compromised across a wider area, there is a greater risk of the veneer becoming loose or detaching entirely, particularly under biting forces. A dentist can assess the degree of debonding and advise on whether monitoring, repair, or replacement is most appropriate in your individual case.

mainEntity.name: Why does my tooth feel sensitive near the veneer margin?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sensitivity near a veneer margin often indicates that dentine — the layer beneath the enamel — has become exposed. This can occur when gum recession pulls the gum tissue away from the veneer edge, revealing an area of the tooth that was previously covered. Dentine contains tiny tubules connected to the nerve of the tooth, which is why exposed dentine can produce sensitivity to temperature, sweet foods, or air. A dentist can assess the cause and suggest appropriate management, which may include desensitising treatments, margin repair, or gum care.

mainEntity.name: How long should dental veneers last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Porcelain veneers are generally considered a long-lasting cosmetic restoration, and with appropriate care many patients maintain their veneers successfully for ten years or more. However, longevity varies considerably between individuals depending on factors such as oral hygiene habits, diet, bruxism (teeth grinding), and the biting forces placed on the veneers. Composite resin veneers tend to have a shorter lifespan than porcelain. No specific lifespan can be guaranteed, and routine monitoring by a dental professional is important to assess the ongoing condition of veneers over time.

mainEntity.name: Should I try to fix a gap around my veneer at home?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is not advisable to attempt to repair a veneer margin at home using over-the-counter adhesives or dental repair kits. These products are not designed for use with porcelain or composite veneer restorations and may make subsequent professional repair more difficult. They can also potentially trap bacteria beneath the veneer margin if applied incorrectly. If you notice a gap, sensitivity, or change around your veneer, the most appropriate course of action is to contact your dental practice to arrange a clinical examination.
